titleStmt.title: Interview with Dallas Smith, Jr., May 15, 2003
titleStmt.author: Thomas A. Swope

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Dallas Smith, Jr. was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Dallas D. Smith, Jr. Mr. Smith served in the U.S. Navy. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Smith's home in Perry, Ohio on May 15th, 2003. Dallas was 82 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Let's see now. We were living up on Route 20 in a tenant house that belonged to Champion Nurseries.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: And it's right about where Champion Garden Town is now if you're familiar with that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So is that in Perry still?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yep, yeah. Yeah, it's in Perry Township. Perry Village is still south of us. We were in Perry Township here.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Let's see. I was just 82 yesterday. So how old was I?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Sixty years ago, 22 -- when were you born?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you were about twenty years old?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: My math is a little slow.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: We were not living on Route 20.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: That's when the -- Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That was going to be my next question.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Well, we were on Antioch Grove.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: We were down at the Antioch.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: And this was also a tenant house of a farmer down there. Our first house, in fact, after we married, the first one we rented. We lived with my folks for a time when we first married.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So were you married in 1941 then?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You got married in 1939?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Uh-huh, right out of school.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I was down in -- I worked at the Diamond alkali (ph) on shift work. It was on a Sunday, of course, and our boss of the department I worked in -- in Department L, which was the chlorine department at the Diamond alkali at the time -- our boss was in the plant that day for some reason or another and he came around -- it was in the afternoon. I don't know it seems to me like it was maybe 1:30 or 2:00, and he -- all the guys, he'd stop and talk. He says, Guys we've got bad news. He said the Japs just bombed Pearl Harbor, you know. Well, then we all get together and we talk; well, that's no big deal. The Navy will be after those yahoos in no time and blow them right out of existence, you know. Everybody thought the Navy was just going to eliminate Japan right now. Well, of course, that didn't happen and we know why now.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How soon after that did you realize how serious the attack was?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Well, of course, not -- I didn't really realize it until we were home, or I was home, and you listen to radio. We didn't have TV then. We listened to radio and all the news, and of course the newspapers and everything. We used to buy the Sunday paper and, of course, that was full of routine news. There was no indication at all, you know. Then the next day in the paper was great big headlines. We might still have one of them around here yet. Do we?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: It was downstairs.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Of Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: And I could have told you right where it was, but --

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Now you can't.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: I can't now. Skip has moved things.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: It was all, you know, we all thought that our country was invisible back then even though it wasn't, and I guess we probably really -- if any of us had been really honest, we would have admitted, you know. When you think about guys going in the service, and this was, of course, the draft was in effect then and we had some friends that we had gone to school with that were drafted early into the Army and they're training with wooden guns. So this will give you an indication. We aren't as well off as we think we are, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So did you have any feeling that we would be dragged into the war before that happened?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Not before really, but it didn't -- I don't know. We never did or never thought too much about it really. You read the news. You listened to all of it, and it just never seemed like Hitler was strong enough to do anything that would drag us into it. And we used to have a barber in town; his name was Al Libs (ph). He was a German and he was born in Germany and he came over here as a kid. He lived in Cleveland, and then he came out from Cleveland as just a real young man and he had gone to barber school in Cleveland and came out here and opened a barber shop. Well, we used to -- of course, everybody got their hair cut over there, and when Hitler was in his heyday from '38 on, you know, I was continually jumping on this guy about the Germans, and he listened to Hitler's speeches on the radio -- well, we did too. You heard him on the radio and you thought, well, this guy is a madman, you know. But you never really thought -- or we didn't anyway really think that this guy is ever going to carry out all of this stuff that he did eventually, and then little by little when he starts overrunning countries like Poland and the other little countries, then you begin to think, well, gee, maybe things are going to be tough. But I never really got -- I don't know, never got wrapped up in it until we got in it.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember listening to FDR's speech on the next day, on December 8th?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, well, I don't think we ever missed any of his speeches, and I voted for FDR the first time he ran for office if I remember -- no, I didn't either because I wasn't old enough, yeah, but the second time; and I voted for him once when I was in the service.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did many of your coworkers decide to go out and enlist after Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, there were a few. And even I did. A friend of mine and I were going to go and enlist in the Merchant Marine and we even went into Cleveland one day. Took off from work and drove into Cleveland to the -- I forget the office downtown. I think it was around Ninth Street someplace. There was a maritime -- had to do with maritime affairs. And we got down there and the place was closed. So we just threw up our hands, turned around, and came back home, went to work the next day. Well, that idea disappeared, you know. I often wondered about what would have happened had I been able to get into the Merchant Marine. I had a guy that I worked with after -- I worked at the Rayon during the war. I left the Diamond after two years and went to the Rayon simply because the Rayon was paying more money than the Diamond was. And this man was a pipe fitter at the Rayon and he was -- I don't know if he enlisted. I never did know for sure if he enlisted in the Merchant Marine or what, but he was a third officer on a merchant ship during the war, and he had left the Rayon in the early -- even before Pearl Harbor if I'm not mistaken to go into the Merchant Marine. And he went through some awful times from his tales. They sailed the route from the east coast to Russia through the North Sea, which was -- Murmansk, I think, was the port that he went to, and he told us horrendous tales of sailing up there, but I don't know. I was never really too much concerned with anything about the war or whatever until I got my notice from -- greetings from Franklin Delano, and I was married and had four children and I thought there's just no way they're ever going to draft me, you know, but they did.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So when did you get that notice?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: 1944? I got the notice in '43, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: No. I was in the hospital. I had just given birth to John.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: My God, I guess that's right.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: April 20th is when he was born.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Were you deferred before that because of your family?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I guess --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: They weren't choosing men with --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: They were taking the single men first?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. They weren't picking -- I didn't really get deferred. I just wasn't --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: They were in a category that they weren't picking.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: They hadn't reached me yet.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: But his age, you know, he was young and --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah. But in my -- I had an uncle that was on the draft board, the local draft board, and he apologized to me and apologized. He said, I'm sorry, we just can't not take you.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah? So you were drafted into the Army?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: I went in the Navy. I had a choice.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: And I asked for the Navy thinking that I'm probably going to get put in the Army just like everybody else was. All the guys that were with me at the time, I don't know, probably more than half of them asked for the Navy and they all, Army -- the guy with the stamp -- Army, Army, and they came to me and they stamped it Navy and I could never figure out exactly why did they do that, you know, and I was thrilled to death because I really wanted to go into the Navy if I had to have a choice. But it was fun kind of. It was a little bit horrendous at first, but I thought, my God.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So what can you tell me about your training then?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I went to Great Lakes and -- for boot camp. And boot camp at the time was only four weeks, four and a half weeks I guess all totaled up. Normally boot camp in the Navy was about 16 weeks. Well, they were so anxious to get guys on ships and whatnot that they had cut the time down about three times up to that point, and then suddenly it was down to four weeks, you know, and it's about time enough for you to learn to salute and say yes, sir and no, sir and do a right face and a left face, about face or whatever, and away you went. And, of course, they gave you all kinds of tests and I took all these tests and some of them were -- well, one of them they called a GCT, which was a general classification. And I asked after I had completed boot camp or I was about to complete, I said, I'd like to go in the Armed Guard, which was a gun crew that they were using on merchant ships. And they said, well, we can't send you there because that Armed Guard school is full. I said, okay, then I'd like to go and do the Navy Air as a machine gunner, a rear seat machine gunner. You know, here's this young stuff coming out, and no, you can't go there because that school is full. And there was some other school I wanted to go to that was full; machinist mate school. The result of this GCT test put me in a service school and I had to go whether I wanted to or not. I didn't even want to go to school, you know. I had already been in school. That's enough school. No, you have to go to school. Okay. So the only school that had openings was the electrician mate school, and that was taught in three places at the time. One was in Purdue University, one was in Iowa State, and the other was at Great Lakes, and it was a 16-week school. You went to school for eight hours a day. Of course, you did all your physical training as well on your off time and that's all you did. And I wanted to go to either one of the college towns. I thought, gee, that will be great to go to a college town. Nope, I go to Great Lakes. Right where I was, you know. Well, that was all right. It was a good school. It was electrician mate school, and supposedly when you graduated from electrical school you're to come out of there as a Third Class Petty Officer. Well, by the time I get through the 16 weeks, they got more Third Class Petty Officers than they know what to do with. So now you're going to be a Fireman First Class, which is the same thing as a Seaman First Class, only one is above deck and one is below deck. So, okay. They said, well, you'll be a Third Class Petty Officer in no time. So -- and I finished service school and they kept a whole gang of us up there in Great Lakes working in an office. It was a payroll office actually. We were filling out all kinds of papers on guys' payrolls, whatever you called it. I forget what they called it; disbursement office. So I worked in that place along with these other guys, a couple of them were friends of mine. I think I was there for a month working in that place and it was good duty as far as, you know, really easy and we -- they got all through with that and they decided you're going to go to Paradise Creek, which was in Newport News, Virginia, and from there you'll be shipped out overseas somewhere. They didn't know where at the time. So I go down there and in the meantime they decide they're going to put me in amphibious training in Little Creek, Virginia, which is right near Newport News and Norfolk and Little Creek are all in a bunch down there. Little Creek is still their amphibious. So they send me to amphibious training in Little Creek. I was going to be an electrician on an LST, which that was kind of interesting. We did some cruising on an LST outside of Chesapeake Bay and down the coast halfway to Florida and back and that sort of thing. That was my first taste of submarine contact out there off of Cape Hatteras.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Ours or theirs?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: It was their submarine, and we're on our ship, of course, doing our training and scared to death, the whole gang of us. God almighty, we didn't know what was going to happen next.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did somebody spot a periscope?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, they spotted a periscope, or they thought it was. We never were attacked. So it could have been something else, you know. But no one ever really knew, but you all went to general quarters, and my battle station on that LST was a 20 millimeter cannon on the main deck. And to get to it was -- the actual position was right over -- above the bunk I slept in, my quarters, and I crawled out through a hatch manhole up to the top deck to take my battle station, and all I have on is my underwear and a life jacket and I'm up there waiting. Don't know what I'm going to do next, you know. Well, after awhile they had an all-clear and we all go back to bed. So that was interesting. And then I finished amphib school, go back to this Paradise Creek layout which was in connection with the shipyard down there in Newport News, and they used to come every day to the barracks where we were. This barracks was like a huge, big place and it was full of guys that were in the process of being shipped out somewhere. And they'd come every day to pick up a load of guys and take them to the shipyard to chip barnacles or do whatever, and they'd come around with one of these big -- like a big school bus only it was Navy. Well, by the time they got down to the shipyard, there wouldn't be anybody left on the bus, you know. They went out the back door as fast as an opportunity because they didn't want to go chip barnacles. But anyway, that time went by and finally they sent me overseas to Oran, Algeria, which was a supply depot, a Navy supply depot.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When did you go overseas then?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: I was onboard ship on Easter -- let's see. It would have been '45, wouldn't it?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Probably Easter, '45.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You went in in April of '44?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So what was that crossing like?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Nothing -- nothing spectacular other than we passed a convoy en route to England on the way in. I never saw so many ships in my life. They used to tell us or you'd hear newsmen on the radio or you'd read in the paper about these convoys going to England, you know. Well, we passed one because the ship we were on was a Navy tanker and we were traveling with another troop ship and they were very -- they were new ships and they could go -- well, we cruised at 17 knots, which was way beyond the normal cruising speed of any of those convoys and that's why we passed them. But everywhere you looked and as far as you could see in any direction was a ship. So that was quite a sight. But nothing happened so, you know, there was -- and we got over to the Straits of Gibraltar and we got into a hurricane. There was a hurricane in progress and we went right through the hurricane. We had 80-mile-an-hour winds and waves that were just unbelievable, you know, mountains of water and this ship just plowed -- and the fact that it was a tanker, the construction of a tanker then was like, well, they had a well deck they called it and the well deck was very near the -- like maybe ten feet above the surface of the water normally because it's just like a big tank. On one end of it is crews' quarters and the bridge and the captain lived there and the foksail they called it on the stern is where the mess hall was and some of the crew lived and the engineering people lived and so forth, but -- and in between this is a catwalk from one of these places to another over the top of the well deck and we would -- in this storm we would be -- if we happened to be at the stern for lunch or breakfast or whatever, you'd have to pick your way between the waves to make it back up to the foksail because the water is going right over that ship, you know. So that was an interesting thing, but it was fun.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Would you like some coffee?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: No, I'm okay. I'm fine. I drink too much coffee.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: But we got over there and got into Oran and docked and they took us off -- there were several of us who were on this ship that were destined for the base there in Oran. We weren't really crew of the ship, although we worked on it just the same as a crew did going over there. But this camp that they took us to was like a receiving area and it was tents and they hauled us up there in trucks and they were six-by-six trucks and they hauled us all up there and we slept in those tents for about three or four days I guess. While we were in the tents, we had a sand storm. It didn't blow the tents down but they all opened up, the sides, you know, so the wind went right through them and God, the dirt. I had two of the nicest blankets issued to me when I went in the Navy, nice white Navy wool blankets, really beautiful, and I was so proud of them things and I washed them and took care of them and kept them because I wanted to bring them home, you know. They were really -- well, I brought them home and they were what color? About the color of these walls, weren't they, Mother, from the dust. And she washed those things and washed them and washed them. Never could get that crap out of them, that African dust. But then they finally -- after they got everybody organized, they put us in kwanza hunts. Different groups went wherever, and I wound up driving a truck over there in Oran and I drove -- well, I drove everything. I drove station wagons and chauffeured officers around. I drove weapon carriers and six-by-sixes. I never once used my electrical training for anything, you know, not unless you call screwing in a light bulb. But -- and they didn't seem to care much. That was -- they needed a truck driver and I could do it and that was it. And, of course, when the war ended in Europe everybody was just elated out of their skull and there was more cheering and whistle blowing and noises. Every ship in the harbor blew their whistles and they just went bananas, you know. And soon after that orders came around that everyone on the base who was married and had dependents is going home to be discharged. And sure enough, it wasn't too many days after that then the ship pulls into Oran and we all get orders, gather up your junk and get down on that boat. It took us sixteen days to come back because it was an old -- well, it wasn't old. It was a liberty ship that had been turned into a troop carrier. What a mess that was. Oh, that was the awfulest (ph) thing. They had guys in a hole sleeping, and if I remember right, they were sixteen high in bunks and some of them had never been on a ship before and they were sick. A lot of these guys were Army soldiers. They had come from Italy and I guess some of them even from Germany. And they stopped in Oran and picked up us guys as sailors that were there. There was a continuous crap game and a poker game on the hatch covers of that ship all the way back to the States. Some of those guys never left. They either lost all the money they had or they won everybody else's or whatever. So it was an interesting crossing. It took us sixteen days to come back, and I can remember the -- we were getting close to Norfolk. We came back into Norfolk, Virginia. We were getting close and it was raining and storming and really a lousy day -- sort of like it has been around here for -- and all of a sudden the storm clears and the sun comes out and there's the lighthouse at Fort Story, Virginia, the flag flying up there, you know. It was really something.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you have much contact with the Algerian people when you were in Algeria?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, a lot of -- they all -- they're the ones that did our work. The Algerians as well as Arabs. We had a lot of Arab people that worked for us. Every bit of work we did of any kind, physical labor of any kind, was done by those people. We didn't do nothing. Like me driving the truck and I'd haul a load of these guys somewhere and have them, you know, doing whatever. We also had a prisoner of war camp right next to our camp that was all Italian prisoners of war and they did all of our cooking, the baking. Every bit of cooking that was done for the whole base was done by these guys and they did -- some of them did some other jobs of some kind or another. And I got to know several of those guys and they were really interesting to know, you know. We used to spend hours sitting and talking with them and showing them pictures of where I lived, my home, and what it was like back here in the States, and these guys couldn't believe it. They had been in the Army since way back in the '30s, you know. Mussolini had put them in the Army and they never had known -- they had been away from home, been down there in North Africa for years and years and didn't know anything. It was interesting to talk to them. Some of them couldn't speak English; they could understand a little bit. And some of them couldn't understand a lot of English and speak good English. So it was fun to talk with them, but yeah, I had a lot of contact with French people. There were a lot of French people and Belgium people there and Algiers. The Arabs were -- I never did trust them. I still don't. I wouldn't trust one from here to that wall, and I hope you're not Arab.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: But I don't know, they just -- they did so many little things and they'd steal the pennies off of -- we used to go into town on liberty every now and then and we'd be wearing dress uniforms and have shined shoes and you'd go downtown and you'd meet with a whole passel of little kids about yay big, and they got shoe shine kits. A little box and bunch of -- and when you're not looking one of them would smear your shoes up with some kind of dye or red stuff or something a different color than black, of course, and then they'd want to sell you a shoe shine. Well, you've got to do something because -- so you'd pay them two or three hundred francs or something like that to shine your shoes or clean your shoes. And if you had a wristwatch, it would be gone. How they got it off, I don't know. More guys lost good wristwatches, stuff in your pockets. Anything in your pockets they would get. So you learn real fast if you're going to town don't have any kind of jewelry or whatever in sight, you know. Just leave it back here on the base, and if you think you might need a couple hundred francs, that's all you take. So you learn that stuff real quick. But generally the people were easy to get along with. They were decent people, you know, and they were all concerned about pretty much the same things we were concerned about. But it was -- there was an air base right near us that the Army or the Air Force flew cargo out of a lot and -- mostly cargo. There was more -- they came in there from different places and then went on up into Italy, and of course, at the time they weren't going to Germany, but every now and then while we were there German Air Force would send reconnaissance planes over, fly over us, and of course east of us the Germans had been in the desert, you know, with Rommel and Montgomery and all that and there had been some big battles close to us. There weren't any while we were there, but there had been some. There was one area that was just outside of town a little ways, they had a big tank battle in the early part of the war and some of the old burned out tanks and stuff were still there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Was there much souvenir collecting of --

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, there was a lot of guys, they were always looking for guns, German guns of some kind or jewelry or anything that was German they were looking for. But not as much, I guess, as you would think. Most of it was stuff you had to buy from some other guy. Some guy had -- like, soldiers sometimes would come in going through town for whatever, on their way to someplace else, and maybe they had P38 pistols or they had Mauser rifles or they had some German insignia of some kind and they'd be selling it to somebody, but nobody -- I don't remember anybody ever going out to the battlefields and really looking for souvenirs. But the only souvenirs I brought home from over there were French money, coins. I still got some laying around here I guess. I brought a shell, an empty shell that was on our -- I guess I didn't bring that from over there though. I had that before. It was on our LST. It was anti aircraft shell that we had been firing. But souvenir-wise, I don't know. I was not really too interested in souvenirs. Possibly had I been in the Army and out in the battlefield someplace, I might have been, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you get much entertainment, USO shows or anything like that coming through?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: We had a couple of shows. They weren't the top notch shows because I don't remember any of the people that were -- at the time that were the so-called stars like Bob Hope or his class, you know. They were people in the entertainment field, but they were -- they didn't mean anything to me. I didn't even know them before then, you know. So it was -- but they were good shows. I mean, they were entertaining and they had gals dancing and singing and the jokers and all that stuff; the usual. They were good shows. They weren't -- their name wasn't Bob Hope or somebody like that instead of -- Thomas A. Swope:: You probably got a lot of your war news through news reels, things like that, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. We had some -- we had movies occasionally.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: And had war news. Most of it was published right through the higher-ups in the base, the officers, and they'd issue bulletins about something, you know. If there were battles that we might be interested in because we were shipping stuff out of our place up north into Germany, or someplace to be used in Germany, because by the time I was there they had already whooped the Italians in Italy, you know. So there wasn't much going on in Italy except occupation.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: As far as the news that you did get, did you believe you were getting an accurate account of what was happening or did you think maybe it was a propaganda slant or --

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I -- yeah, I think we figured that it was probably pretty accurate.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Some of it is baloney because, you know, I think these people that relate the news, that's part of their training is to be able to spread a little baloney in with the news. They still do that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: But I think in general everybody, you know, accepted that whatever we got, we heard, that was on the up and up. And we got -- we had all kinds of ships come in there from the States. Military would come in there to resupply or they came in for whatever, brought stuff in to unload at the dump, the depot, and so we got a lot of information from the crew on those ships about what's going on. We used to always try to get on when a U.S. Merchant ship would come in and we had to unload whatever they had. We'd try to get on the ship, of course, and get up to the mess hall and get stuff because they always had a lot of good eats, you know. Different than ours. Man, some of them ships really ate good. And we'd have our Arabs or Frenchmen unloading doing the scut work and we were on board.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Was the food at the base any good --

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: -- when the Italians cooked it?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: In general, yeah, they were. You know, the best thing they had, when they made spaghetti it was unbelievable. It was out of this world. I can see why the Italians are renown for spaghetti. They made it from scratch. They made the dough and they had a big press that they ran it through to make the -- and it was really good. But generally, yes, the food we had was excellent in the Navy compared -- we always had a lot of Army guys and the first thing they wanted was something to eat because they got better stuff to eat from us than they did in their own outfits, and the Navy always was noted for better chow anyhow from -- even here in the States, up there in Great Lakes. My God we ate -- we just -- we ate the best of everything. And some guys, of course, would gripe about beans and that sort of thing, you know, but man, I made out like a bandit with the beans because I just love baked beans; still do.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How about mail call? Do you remember getting letters or packages from your wife?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, V-mail.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: V-mail?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: We used to get a lot of V-mail. She wrote --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: I wrote every night.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: And I'd get a whole stack of those. Of course, it came in bunches. But I don't remember you sending me anything overseas, did you, packages?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: She sent me stuff up at Great Lakes while I was there and all I got was the package that it came in, you know. It would be empty. Like cookies and stuff like that. She sent me a basket of apples once because I liked apples and she sent this basket up there and all I got was the basket. There wasn't an apple left.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: And they didn't just fall out, right?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: No, no, no. That's what they said. They said, well, the package must have come open in the transit. Yeah, it came open all right.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Didn't I send you an angel food cake overseas?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Maybe, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You don't know if you got it? It never made it?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: No, I think most of the stuff -- everything that she sent over there got over there. It seemed to me like it did.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: I bought a tin box.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Went up to the place there in Painesville and bought a tin box to make a care package.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: It had cookies and all different -- playing cards and I don't know what else I had in there, cigarettes.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, that's right. I was smoking cigarettes then. Of course, they were a nickel a pack in the ship store, you know, and then we used to get them -- every now and then we'd get a carton from some union or something. There would be a tag or a card in it, This carton was donated by local so and so and so, The United Auto Workers or whoever, and they would pass those out. And the Red Cross had a place over there in Oran that we could go to for -- oh, we'd get stuff to eat, sandwiches and Coke and cigarettes and sit around and read magazines and they'd give you help if you were having problems with, oh, something going on at home, like you lost somebody at home and that sort of thing. They had people over there. But they lived pretty high on the hog those Red Cross people and they charged you for all that stuff that they were supposed to give you.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. I never got anything free from the Red Cross.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Never.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Just pocketed the money?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: I don't know what they did. I suppose, and it wasn't much. Like a baloney sandwich should be -- or a Spam sandwich, which our base gave them the Spam to start with for free, you know, but they would -- it was all served nice and they made nice sandwiches and everything, but you paid ten cents a piece for them or twenty cents or something like that. A Coke would be ten cents. That stuff was all donated to them by the government I suppose. I'm sure that every place there was a base of any kind they got that sort of -- but then towards the end of the war in Europe, we used to get -- I remember one time we got a whole liberty ship full of beer and you can't imagine how many cases of beer that is. Rupert's Beer, and it wasn't worth pouring out on the ground, you know. But everybody drank it just the same. And, of course, the base had a big party and a beer party and they had -- I forget. They had stuff to -- like a picnic, hot dogs and all that stuff. So they -- but the beer was sent over there by -- we thought it was the Jacob Rupert Brewing Company just gave it to us. (END OF CD NO. 1) (BEGIN CD NO. 2) It was well received. A lot of guys practically took a bath in it. Because we never got any good beer. The French beer that was available was awful. The most alcoholic beverages of any kind over there were wine, of course. The French were notorious for wine, and the Arabs didn't have anything like that, but the --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you first went into the Navy, was it a tough adjustment to be thrown into a situation with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, a little bit, but I don't know, you -- after you're in there awhile you realize that the other guys are just as disrupted as you are as far as where they came from, you know. Most of them were from farm areas. A lot of guys I was in boot camp with came from Minnesota. Our company commander was a teacher, a school teacher from Iowa. And so they were the same kind of guys as us, you know, the whole company, the boot company, Company 1095. And we -- it didn't take long so you get, you know, you get friendly with everybody, you know. It really wasn't a tough deal. Maybe at the time some of us thought it was because we were -- didn't want to leave home in the first place, but we had to go and so you thought -- but after you're there awhile and -- I think probably the most disruptive thing of the whole deal when you first go in -- now, like myself I got on a train in Painesville, go into Cleveland, go through doctors examinations, and military examinations are something else, and you get on another train and head for Chicago. You get to Chicago and they take us all off of that train and put us on another train to Great Lakes. You get to Great Lakes and the first thing you do is you go down to the building where they issue uniforms and they instruct you what to do with your clothes you're wearing at the time. You put them in this box and you write on this label where they go, your home address and all this. And there you're standing with nothing on, no clothes, and they start handing you stuff, Navy uniforms, and they -- one guy takes your shoe size and paints it on your belly with Mercurochrome or something like that and another guy has got your shirt size and he puts that down someplace. It's all written on you, you know. So when you go through the line, the guy that's issuing is looking at that and he's passing it all out. Every now and then you get the wrong size something. Like one of my pairs of pants, white pants I think they were, was a size -- God, it wouldn't fit some small kid even, you know, and I got -- we got to our barracks and I'm putting this stuff -- or looking at it, how the hell am I ever going to wear that, you know. Well, I couldn't. So you go back and go through a whole bunch of rigamarole exchanging it. But that probably was when you were sort of designated nothing, you know, and you're treated like an animal or something, and this is probably really the toughest part of the whole -- but after you get all your stuff and then some guy starts telling you how you -- in the Navy you roll your clothes so they go in a sea bag because that's what you keep all your stuff in is a sea bag. So you learn how to do all this. And it's kind of interesting when you think about it. And it's surprising how nice they look after being packed like that. You think, this will look like hell, but it doesn't. And so you learn all those things as you go along in boot camp and, of course, you learn your right foot from your left foot. And I was a tall guy, so I'm one of the first ones -- there are three -- they line you up in three ranks, or boot company, and the tall guys are up front and they graduate you then. They start you out pretty good so you're -- well, they started out teaching you how to march and about face and all that stuff. So that's -- that's a little bit, oh, I don't know. I don't know how to describe it. It's kind of, you think, why me, you know?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: But I was lucky maybe more than some of them because I had been to a YMCA camp when I was a kid and we had done a little bit of that stuff in YMCA camp. Well, then I had been to Boy Scouts. I used to belong to the Boy Scouts. So we did some of that in the Boy Scouts. So I had an inkling in the back of my mind what this is all about to start with, you know. So it helped. Any of the guys that never had done any of that, they were -- they had two left feet, and I mean two left feet, and they were constantly getting harangued by the company commander how dumb they were and all this, you know. And I could see where that would be hard to take. Especially when maybe you're older than the guy that's doing it, you know. Because all of our guys weren't young like I was. Some of them were old men. And, I mean, they really weren't old men. They were old compared to me, but -- and I can understand how they would resent having some young guy call them stupid and all this; you don't know your right foot from your left and whatever. But boot camp was interesting. I've often said I think since then, and I told my own boys, that's what you need is about four weeks in boot camp, you know. And I think that's great. I think you learn a lot of things and you learn respect for a lot of things that you don't have otherwise. So I don't resent any of it. In fact, when I was discharged the officer that filled out my discharge papers, he says, I think you should stay in the Navy. He said, you have good intelligence and you have a good record and everything and this is going to be a great career for you if you want to do it, you know. He says, in twenty years' time, you know, you can retire and you're still a young man. And I've kicked myself ever since I didn't do exactly that. But who knows. At the time, let me out of here, I want to go home.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When did you finally get home?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: I was home in 1945. In November, wasn't it, Ma?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Yep. You were home for Thanksgiving.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you got back?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, God, it was so great. And the kids were tickled to see me. Of course, the kids weren't too sure who I was even.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Well, John didn't know you.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: No, he was too little. But the other three kids were -- but it was fun. Oh, I don't know, and then the holidays were coming up and Christmas and we had so much fun with all that stuff, and it just seemed like a person with kids, a family person, is supposed to be home with a family, not in the service. But I've thought about it many times since that I would have been better off maybe financially and as far as retirement if I had stayed in until I could retire because I know people that did exactly that and went -- served their time and retired and, for instance, you can go and work in the post office and get a heck of a good job, you know, and retire from the post office. And the benefits from all that are fabulous. And the medical benefits alone are worth so much that -- and today to go -- now, I'm entitled to VA benefits, but to go through that is -- I might as well take a walk out here in the woods someplace, you know. I get better -- I already tried that once and--

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Too much hassle?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, I just said I don't need this.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You mentioned Christmas, and I've always thought about this, was Christmas 1945 maybe the best Christmas that you remember?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: The first postwar Christmas.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: I probably -- yeah, I probably would say that because, you know, just getting home and the kids and -- I think probably it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I'm just curious about that. It would just seem that everybody must have been in a really good mood that Christmas.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, that's right. I think so because, you know, when the war ended with Japan, why everybody just went bananas with the -- so happy that this is all over with and all these guys are going to get to come home and everything, but I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during World War II, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?Dallas Smith, Jr.:: No, I don't know. I had some pretty good experiences. Gee, I don't know. Any particular one that was better than the other? They were interesting in --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Well, anything that comes to mind.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Some of them were fun and --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you have close buddies?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, we had friends that I was in service school with, electrical school, and they lived in Indiana and we used to go back and forth. Well, his wife and Nadine used to come to Chicago when they could on a weekend and we'd have the weekend off and, you know, all of a sudden after the war was over -- this guy worked for General Motors Corporation and he was an electrician before he went in the Navy. So electrical work was his -- he knew more about electrical work than most of those guys that were trying to teach him something else, you know. All of a sudden, we used to send cards back and forth and we used to go visit. We went to his house once and they came here with their kids and we went there with ours, and all of a sudden we don't hear anything from either one of them, and we've sent cards and letters and they all come back. Just like they were all dead, and I don't know if they are or not. We never did do anything really to find out. It was kind of oh, I don't know, sort of hurt a little bit, you know, to lose track of him like that. But they were the only ones that we really ever knew very well, weren't they, Mother?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Any of the other guys, most of them were -- there were several of them from Minnesota --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: The last contact we had was when we went up to Indiana when John was in the -- playing football for college. Dallas Smith, Jr.:: Our youngest son went to school at Ohio Northern and he played football and basketball there and they were playing out in Indiana at Ball State I think it was, which is out near Anderson where these people lived, or it's in that area. So we thought, we'll go to the football game and then we'll look them up on the way back, you know. Couldn't find hind or hair of them. Then they just -- like they disappeared. But other than -- I don't know anything that happened -- after you're gone I'll think of a whole bunch.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I know, it always happens. Well, this is the free form part. If you think of anything you want to bring up that I haven't asked about, anything else from that time.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. Gosh, I don't know of anything really that -- that was a -- working at the Rayon after the Diamond I was in a pipe fitter crew down there at the Rayon and, God, they were all just fabulous people. When I got drafted, they had a party for me. They gave me little stuff, presents, pen and pencil set and this kind of stuff, and the plant manager said, Now when you come back, don't forget, your job is going to be right here. We want to see you when you come home on leave or whatever, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: You come down here, we want to see you. And I did do that. And they were -- they treated me like I was General So-and-So and won the war, you know. But that was always stuck in my mind. It was -- to be that well thought of by a group like that. And, God, now that I think about it, most of those people are dead. That's quite awhile ago. But it was interesting. And the things that -- well, of course they all wanted to know, you know, what you did and how many ships you sunk and how many Japs you shot and all this. This was a big thing with everybody and, of course, I was just far enough down the line as going into it that the big battles were over with and the -- so there wasn't any fantastic action or anything like that that you could talk about or remember. We used to laugh when we talked about the battle of Great Lakes and that kind of -- but I'd like to go -- I have a great grandson that just went through Great Lakes and now he's down in Pensacola in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: And he's in some kind of computer school set up down there. I don't know exactly what it is because Pensacola is a Navy flight school. My youngest son went there. He enlisted in the Navy and they sent him to Pensacola. He learned to fly there and he did a stretch in it. So they -- interesting, I have a grandson in law that just finished a stretch in the Navy and he was in a nuclear submarine. It's fun to talk to him to hear the stuff that he -- while I was at Great Lakes they had -- they used to build submarines up in Wisconsin, Manitowoc, Wisconsin. And they brought them down through Lake Michigan and into the Chicago River and down the Mississippi and, of course, turned them over to the Navy somewhere. And on the way down they'd stop at Great Lakes with a new sub, you know, and they were trying to recruit submariners and I was right on the verge of volunteering for some reason. I was so fascinated by that submarine and, of course, those were -- the World War II were nothing like the nukes are today. But the other guys, you go down -- we all went and toured this new sub, of course, and they thought I was a nut, you know. What the hell do you want to be in something like this for, you know, and not that I know of did they ever get anybody to volunteer. But I was right on the verge and I -- the only thing that stopped me was the thought of her and these four kids at home, and I thought, I got no business being in something like that, you know, because the submarines were -- our submarines were not fairing too well during the war. They lost a lot of submarines. Especially in the Pacific, which is probably where I would have gone. But it was -- but I was so fascinated by the machinery and the -- and the things they do, you know, on a submarine that -- but -- and, of course, trying to get in all that other stuff. No, that's full, that's full, you can't go there. You can't do this. You've got to do what we want. So I did. And I don't regret a bit of it. I was tickled to death that I was able to go and do it. And I'd do it again in a minute. And I just wished I had stayed in there until I had in twenty years or even thirty years. I have a son-in-law who spent twenty-seven years in the Air Force and I see what his benefits are because he was in the Air Force. The medical alone and -- it's just unbelievable. (A telephone rings in the background.)

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: If they want me, tell them I'm busy. The history teacher over here at the high school had a program with his junior and senior history classes and they invited veterans through the American Legion Post here in Perry that I belong to to come over and talk to their kids; like four kids, five kids in a group and then one or two of us guys, veterans, to talk to them and to answer any questions they got about what it was like during the war, what we did before, what it was like being in the service, this kind of thing, and it was the most fun and it was so interesting, and I was really -- my opinion of teenagers changed because of that. These kids aren't the knuckleheads everybody thinks they are, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: They got a lot on the ball and they're thinking and they want to know this stuff, and it's hard for us to realize there are people that don't even know what you're talking about when you say World War II, you know. That's a term. And these kids were like that. Now, of course, they studied this stuff in history, but so many of them, especially -- well, it wasn't just boys more than girls. I think it was both of them --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: -- were so interested in, well, what did you do, you know, how did you do this?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: And we talked about what it was like to have gas ration and food ration and this kind of stuff. What we were doing before we were drafted or whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So what was that like?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Well, it was horrendous, you know. You get -- if you didn't work in a plant, defense plant, you wouldn't get enough gas hardly to go get your hair cut--

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: I had trouble getting shoes for the children because they grew and they would grow out of them and you only had one coupon, you know. Of course, each one of them had their own coupon, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Their feet would grow so fast?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: And you'd get one pair per year, is that right?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: I don't remember that, but my mother and father didn't use all of their coupons so they would give us their coupons.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Well, one of the things, speaking of grandma, she had the restaurant going and she got different allotments because of flour and sugar and whatever because she's in a business like the restaurant. So she got extra things that would help us, even gasoline. Because they were selling gasoline. Well you think all you've got to do is go over there and fill it up. Well, no, it's not that simple.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: But I would give her sugar coupons because we didn't use the sugar. In a family of four I got quite a bit of sugar surprisingly.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you had more than you could eat.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Well, we just weren't that inclined to eat that much sugar anyways. But it was -- and then you had your --

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: I remember doing just what they're doing. Same kind of gun. That's the empty shell I've got laying around here someplace. I don't know where --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Don't ask me where. Don't ask me where anything is.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: But that was interesting. You know the best gunner that I remember -- you were talking about incidents. When I was in service school at Great Lakes, our barracks were right on the bank of Lake Michigan and down over the bank are a whole bunch of antiaircraft gun emplacements that they used for training, and they'd tow targets over these guys with airplanes. The best gunner -- and she was teaching gunnery. She was a WAF, Navy female -- I forget what her rank was. She wasn't an officer. She was like a petty officer.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: But she was the best one of any of the gunners. When they would come across with their target and she was firing at that thing, she just shot it to pieces.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: But she's teaching these guys all. We used to stand in our barracks and look out the window, you know, because we're looking right out over like, and we'd watch this plane coming with that target, bam, bam, bam, and she just brittles it, but I remember that real plain. These guys -- we used to holler at some of them because we'd see them somewhere on the base and, You guys ought to be ashamed of yourself letting that gal outshoot you. But it was a -- that was a pretty good life really. You know, I could understand why a guy goes in the military and makes a career of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: That's not too bad. Even in war time. Now, I'm sure that a guy who was in -- we'll say Europe, for instance, in the Battle of the Bulge would say, you don't know what the hell you're talking about.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah, they'd refute it; I have no regrets about leaving.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: But generally it was pretty good.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Talk about gas rationing, we had a dog that went rabid and we had to all have shots and we had to go to the doctor once every day and get the shot, and I had four children and they were like --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: They all had to have them. And I went to the gas rationing board to ask for more stamps they had for gasoline and -- no, I didn't. I only had three because John wasn't born yet and --

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: He said, well, get on the bus. It goes right by your house every day. And I said, have you ever tried to take three children on the bus, two of them were twins that were -- well, barely toddlers.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: They were just walking.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Just barely. And I had just been in and had my shot and I was pregnant, and they give them to you all the way around your middle and I got upset and I passed out in the rationing board. I got my stamps.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I guess.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: But in a way it was funny; in a way it was so frustrating. Because I just said I cannot handle these children on the bus and --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: All I needed was just a little gas to go to Painesville, which is six miles; a daily trip of twelve miles.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Wow. Did you get involved in strat (?) guides or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: No, because I was so involved in raising the kids and trying to keep the house.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah, you certainly had --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: And in the meantime I bought this house while he was overseas. No, he hadn't gone overseas yet.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: No, I was still in Great lakes. Yeah, we got evicted from the house that we lived in.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Well, not really evicted. They couldn't do that. That was one of the --

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, but they wanted the house real bad to put --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Help in.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: -- help in to work in the nursery and we weren't helping them. You know, the rent was so -- and she bought this house during the -- well, that was in 1944 because we lived here ever since then. But I was in Great Lakes fighting for my country.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: One of the things they made my father take a job down at the Rayon. My mother and father were running the gas station and the restaurant in combination, and it made it very difficult because then my mother had to do the gas station during the day when my dad had to work and it was some rough times.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Now, they made him take the job or --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Yes. Because he wasn't doing anything for the defense they said.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: They wanted him to do something?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, the war effort.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: He was too old to go to war and so he went to work at the Rayon.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Well, the Rayon was making yarn, tire yarn --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: And yarn that was used in parachutes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Nylon.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Not nylon. That was a bad word at the Rayon.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Oh, that's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Competitor?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: But that was the thing that they were -- oh, I could remember before I went in the service they used to have big shindigs down there. The big shots would come in from -- there would be some Army guys and all kinds of politicians and they'd have these big deals, you know, in the cafeteria and they'd have all this stuff displayed, and the Army would be there with displays of different things that were -- Rayon was used in and then, of course, there would be a jab in the back, don't forget to buy bonds, war bonds.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Where was the Rayon plant?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Down on Bacon Road by the lake. It's still there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do they do anything there?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: No. The Rayon has been gone.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: But the building is still there?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: There for a while the lake tram was using that.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Well, they used part of it as the garage.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: As a garage, before they built the one -- what is that? Where is their garage? Is that Blaze Neiman.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: No, I think their garage is out in Painesville somewhere.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Well, I don't know. But anyways, they did use --

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: They used that one for awhile. Part of it -- the water treatment plant that the Rayon built and used was taken over by the county or bought by the county, and they still use that water treatment plant; the water intake and all that from the lake.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: There's quite an area down there where they planted trees and a little monument of each of the men that gave their lives during the war.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: There were several men there that I knew -- three or four of them I went to school with them, in fact -- that were killed.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Garbin (ph) and Dexter (ph) and Dickie Burko (ph). Well, he didn't work down there though, did he?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: No. But there's another guy from Perry that worked -- I forget his name. It was a big tall guy. But the company planted these oak trees around the entrance driveway into the plant.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: And then at the base of each tree they put a little stone monument and that was for each one of the --Thomas A. Swope:: These are former employees that died during the war?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. And then they had a big monument--

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Are those still there, those monuments?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Yes, they are.

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: As far as I know they are.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Smith
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Because Bill was -- don't you know he -- they were to decide who was supposed to take care of it, the veterans or the township?

sp.speaker: Dallas Smith, Jr.
sp.p: Right. The county -- the county and the veterans organization were hassling back and forth who is going to take care of this because the one big monument that they had down there was a big, oh, about yay high and sort of a stone monument. (END OF INTERVIEW)
